react-dom.example: When a visitor opens the contact page, React draws the contact form onto it.

react-native.whatItIs: A toolkit for building phone apps with JavaScript and React, a library for screen components.
goodAt: Building the same app screens for Android and iPhone
Using a single set of components for both phone systems
notGoodAt: Providing a server or database; you add those separately.
react-native.example: When a user opens the sign-in screen, the phone shows its own text fields and buttons.

react-native-css.whatItIs: Connects CSS stylesheets to React Native styling.

react-native-reanimated.whatItIs: Animation tools for React Native phone screens, such as panels that slide open.
goodAt: Animating a panel or button as a user interacts with it
Linking movement to a user's finger drag on the screen
notGoodAt: Moving between screens; a navigation library handles that.
react-native-reanimated.example: When a user taps the menu icon, the side panel slides into view on the phone instead of jumping.

react-native-safe-area-context.whatItIs: Helps React Native content avoid areas covered by notches and system bars.

react-native-screens.whatItIs: Provides the native screen parts that React Native navigation uses to show each screen.

react-native-web.whatItIs: Lets React Native components run in a web browser, so one set of screens can serve both phone and web.
goodAt: Showing a phone-designed screen in a web browser
Reusing the same screen parts on a phone and a website
notGoodAt: Guaranteeing identical behavior on phones and browsers; test each one.
react-native-web.example: When a designer wants to preview a phone screen on a laptop, the same screen code appears in a browser window.

react-native-worklets.whatItIs: Lets a phone app run small pieces of its code on a separate thread, so animations and gestures stay smooth.

react-router.whatItIs: A framework for building React websites, with pages at set web addresses that load their own data.
goodAt: Linking each page to its web address and the data it needs
Sending a form's answers to the server and showing the result
notGoodAt: Providing user accounts or file storage; add those separately.
react-router.example: Before a page shows one order, the app loads that order's details from the server.

satori.whatItIs: A library that turns a web-style layout, described with text and styles, into an SVG picture.
goodAt: Making social preview cards from a title and a background
Creating pictures that stay sharp at any size
notGoodAt: Making a PNG file by itself; pair it with an image converter.
satori.example: When a site needs a preview picture for an article, it fills a card layout with the article's title.

server-only.whatItIs: A small package that makes a build fail if code meant only for the server ends up in a browser page.
goodAt: Marking a module that talks to a database as server only
Making a mistaken import fail during the build, not after the site is live
notGoodAt: Being the only safeguard; it works only where the build tool checks it.
server-only.example: When a developer accidentally imports a database module into a browser component, the build stops before the site ships.

svelte.whatItIs: Svelte, a tool for building the parts of a web page that respond to users, compiled into browser code when the app is built.
goodAt: Building forms, menus and other page parts that update when a user acts
Keeping a page part's layout and its behavior together in one file
notGoodAt: Serving pages or storing data by itself; add SvelteKit and a database for that.
svelte.example: When a customer changes the quantity on a cart page, the total updates on the screen at once, without a reload.

svelte-check.whatItIs: A command-line checker that reports TypeScript errors in Svelte components and the code around them.

tailwind-merge.whatItIs: A helper that removes clashing Tailwind CSS style names, such as two padding settings on one element.
goodAt: Combining style choices a user picks, such as a button size
Letting a page change a component's default style without a clash
notGoodAt: Creating the style names themselves; Tailwind CSS provides those.
tailwind-merge.example: When a button gets a second padding setting, the helper keeps only the later one.

tailwindcss.whatItIs: A styling toolkit made of small, ready-made style names that you combine on each element.
goodAt: Styling buttons, cards and layouts with short style names
Keeping spacing and colors consistent across a site
notGoodAt: Choosing the look of your site for you; you design the pages.
tailwindcss.example: When a page's buttons need to look dimmer when disabled, one style name sets the faded color.

tsdown.whatItIs: Builds a TypeScript package into the JavaScript and type files that get published, in one fast step.
goodAt: Turning a library's TypeScript code into files ready to publish
Writing the type information other TypeScript projects read
notGoodAt: Building websites or apps; use a web build tool such as Vite for those.
tsdown.example: When a developer finishes a new function, one command writes the publishable code and its types into a dist folder.

typescript.whatItIs: JavaScript with added checks that flag values used the wrong way, before the code runs.
goodAt: Catching a wrong value type before a program is run
Showing a function's expected inputs to other developers
notGoodAt: Checking outside data while the program runs; use a validation library for that.
typescript.example: While a developer writes a price function, the editor warns that a text value was passed where a number belongs.

typescript-eslint.whatItIs: Connects ESLint rules to TypeScript code.

vite.whatItIs: A tool that runs a website on your computer while you edit it, and packages it for publishing.
goodAt: Showing a live preview of a web app while editing it
Packaging a finished website into files ready to publish
notGoodAt: Deciding an app's pages and addresses; a framework does that.
vite.example: While a developer edits a React page, the browser refreshes to show each change right away.

vitest.whatItIs: A testing tool for JavaScript and TypeScript projects that runs automated checks and reports what failed.
goodAt: Running checks on single functions and on parts working together
Checking a server's behavior after each change
notGoodAt: Checking a whole site in a real browser; use browser tests for that.
vitest.example: When a developer changes how shipping is priced, the tests run and report any order that now costs the wrong amount.

vue.whatItIs: Vue, a tool for building the parts of a web page that respond to users, written as components that keep their layout, behavior and style together.
goodAt: Building forms, lists and menus that update when a user acts
Splitting a page into small parts that can be reused and tested
notGoodAt: Serving pages or storing data by itself; add Nuxt and a database for that.
vue.example: When a shopper types in the search box, the list of products below narrows at once, without a reload.

vue-router.whatItIs: The official page-address handling for Vue apps, which shows the right page for each address; Nuxt uses it under the hood.

vue-tsc.whatItIs: A command-line checker that reports TypeScript errors in Vue components and the code around them.

wrangler.whatItIs: A command-line tool for running and publishing small server programs on Cloudflare Workers.
goodAt: Running a server program on your computer before publishing it
Publishing a finished server program to Cloudflare
notGoodAt: Writing the program itself; you write the code.
wrangler.example: Before a team publishes a change, they run the server program on their laptop and check the answers.

yaml.whatItIs: A JavaScript library for reading and writing YAML, a plain-text format for settings and data files.
goodAt: Reading a settings file written in YAML into a program
Writing a program's data back out as a YAML file
notGoodAt: Checking that settings make sense; add your own checks for that.
yaml.example: When the app starts, it reads a YAML settings file and uses the values inside.

zod.whatItIs: A TypeScript library for checking that data has the expected form while the program runs.
goodAt: Checking data a website or phone app sends to a server
Checking settings and data files before a program uses them
notGoodAt: Storing data after it is checked; use a database for that.
zod.example: When someone submits a signup form without an email address, it stops the request and returns a clear error instead of saving an incomplete record.

zustand.whatItIs: A small tool that holds shared app data, such as a filter choice, for React screens to use.
goodAt: Sharing a user's choices between different parts of a page
Keeping a filter selection available across screens
notGoodAt: Keeping server records up to date by itself; use a data-fetching tool for that.
zustand.example: When a shopper picks a price range on the list screen, the same choice still applies on the detail screen.

@nestjs/core.whatItIs: The heart of NestJS, a framework for building servers in TypeScript that splits the code into modules and hands each part what it needs.
goodAt: Larger backends that several developers work on at once
Servers where every feature follows the same layout
notGoodAt: Tiny services with a couple of routes; a lighter toolkit such as Hono is simpler.
@nestjs/core.example: When a team adds an invoices feature, it gets its own module with the same parts as every other feature.

@nestjs/common.whatItIs: The shared building blocks of NestJS, such as the markers that turn a class into a route handler or a service.

@nestjs/platform-express.whatItIs: Lets a NestJS server answer web requests through Express, the long-standing web server library for Node.

@nestjs/config.whatItIs: Reads a NestJS server's settings, such as its port, from the environment and a local .env file, and checks them at startup.
goodAt: Stopping a server at startup when a setting is wrong
Giving every part of the server the same settings
notGoodAt: Keeping secrets safe on its own; use the host's secret storage for that.
@nestjs/config.example: When someone sets the port to a word instead of a number, the server refuses to start and names the setting.

@nestjs/swagger.whatItIs: Describes a NestJS server's endpoints in an OpenAPI document, a standard description of an API, and serves a page to try them.
goodAt: Showing other developers every endpoint and the data it takes
Producing a file that tools turn into ready-made client code
notGoodAt: Checking requests by itself; the server's validation does that.
@nestjs/swagger.example: When a mobile developer needs to know what creating a note takes, they open the docs page and try it there.

@nestjs/cli.whatItIs: The NestJS command line tool, which builds the server and writes new modules, controllers and services in the framework's layout.

@nestjs/schematics.whatItIs: The templates the NestJS command line tool uses when it writes new modules, controllers and services.

@nestjs/testing.whatItIs: Helpers for testing NestJS code, which build a small copy of the server's modules so a test can use or replace their parts.

reflect-metadata.whatItIs: Lets code record notes about its own classes, which NestJS reads to work out what each part needs.

rxjs.whatItIs: A library for handling values that arrive over time, such as events, which NestJS uses inside its request handling.

class-validator.whatItIs: Checks the data a request sends against rules written on a TypeScript class, such as a required title of at most 200 characters.
goodAt: Rejecting bad input before it reaches the server's logic
Telling a caller which field was wrong and why
notGoodAt: Checking data with no class behind it; a schema library such as zod fits better.
class-validator.example: When an app sends a note with an empty title, the server answers with an error naming the title field.

class-transformer.whatItIs: Turns plain request data into instances of TypeScript classes, so their checking rules and default values apply.

@types/express.whatItIs: Type definitions for Express, so TypeScript can check code that uses its requests and responses.

supertest.whatItIs: Sends real web requests to a server inside a test and checks the answers, without starting it by hand.
goodAt: Checking each endpoint's status codes, headers and data
Testing the whole server path from request to response
notGoodAt: Testing pages in a browser; use a browser testing tool for that.
supertest.example: When a developer changes how notes are created, a test posts a note and checks the server answers with the new note.

@types/supertest.whatItIs: Type definitions for supertest, so TypeScript can check tests that use it.

oxlint.whatItIs: A fast checker for JavaScript and TypeScript that points out likely bugs, such as a forgotten await, before the code runs.
goodAt: Catching common mistakes in seconds, even in large projects
Running on every save or commit without slowing work down
notGoodAt: Tidying spacing and line breaks; use a formatter such as Prettier.
oxlint.example: When a developer forgets to wait for a save to finish, the checker flags the line before the change is merged.

oxlint-tsgolint.whatItIs: Adds checks to oxlint that need TypeScript's understanding of the code, such as finding an unawaited promise.
